scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being AITA (A**hole I**n** The** A**ct**) for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money. Let me start by understanding the situation better. First, I'm 21 years old, and I'm in my third year of university, working to put myself through school. I'm in business school, which I find challenging but manageable. I plan to graduate in two years. When I started university, I began saving a portion of my paychecks, sometimes as much as 15% and other times as low as 1%, to go on a big vacation after graduation. My goal is to take a cruise, visit Japan, or travel to different countries in Europe, places I've never been to. Right now, my vacation fund has about $2,800 in it. My brother is 30 and lives with our parents. He's in a bad job and went back to school to try to get out of it, which is why he moved back in 11 months ago. He's been hinting that he needs a vacation, and my parents already help him financially, so he wouldn't ask them for more help for that. Last week, when he was complaining to my parents about needing a vacation, they mentioned my vacation fund and suggested he could have been doing something similar all these years to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. Three days ago, my brother came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or fall. He said since I won't need it for another two years, there's plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do, but he always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I don't pay rent either, which is why I've been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone, and uni fees). He's very mad that I said no. He says it's not fair because, as the youngest child, I get to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it's not fair that I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went, whereas he had to go back. He says I've only been able to save so much money because mom and dad spoiled me. I disagree. My father, as well as my university accounting and finance classes, taught me to budget. If anything, I think my parents spoiled him because he doesn't know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don't think it's fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he'll be able to pay me back in time. Even if he could, I'm uncomfortable with the idea. Am I being AITA for refusing to loan him my vacation money? Alright, so to figure this out, I need to consider a few things: 1. **Financial Responsibility**: Am I being responsible by not lending him money, especially considering his history with money management? 2. **Family Dynamics**: Is there an underlying issue with how our parents treat us differently, and how does that affect our relationship? 3. **Personal Goals**: Is it reasonable for me to prioritize my own vacation plans, especially since I've been saving for it for years? 4. **Potential Consequences**: What could happen if I lend him the money and he doesn't pay it back? How would that affect our relationship? 5. **Alternative Solutions**: Are there other ways he could fund his vacation without borrowing from me? 6. **Emotional Impact**: How does this situation make me feel, and how am I handling my brother's anger? 7. **Long-term Perspective**: How might this decision affect our relationship in the future? 8. **Moral and Ethical Considerations**: Is there a moral obligation to help family members in need, or is it acceptable to prioritize my own goals? 9. **Communication**: Have I communicated my reasons clearly to my brother, or could better communication resolve some of the tension? 10. **Boundaries**: Is setting a boundary by refusing to lend him money a healthy way to protect my financial and emotional well-being? Considering all these factors, I need to weigh the pros and cons of lending him the money versus keeping it for my own use. It's important to think about not just the immediate situation but also how this decision could impact our relationship and my future plans. I also need to reflect on whether my refusal is based on rational reasons or if there's an emotional component influencing my decision. Understanding my motivations can help me make a more balanced choice. Additionally, exploring whether there are other ways to support my brother without jeopardizing my own plans might be a constructive approach. Perhaps discussing alternative solutions with him could alleviate some of the tension and find a middle ground that works for both of us. In summary, to determine if I'm being AITA, I need to evaluate the situation from multiple angles, considering financial, emotional, relational, and ethical perspectives, and decide whether my decision aligns with my values and priorities.
